overview: Under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program, run by the Treasury Department, the federal government pays part of what private insurers owe after a terrorist attack on property and casualty policies, which cover damage to property and legal liability. The program is now set to end on December 31, 2027, and this bill would extend it seven years, to December 31, 2034. In some cases the law requires the Treasury to recover part of its payments later by adding surcharges to property and casualty insurance policies, and the bill would push back those collection deadlines by seven years as well, moving the latest one from September 30, 2029, to September 30, 2036. Nothing else about the program would change, including how much of insurers' losses the government covers.
for: Supporters say the program keeps terrorism coverage available and affordable for businesses and property owners, and that letting it lapse could make it harder to insure or finance large buildings and projects.
against: Critics say the program shifts risk from private insurers to taxpayers, and that extending it again discourages the insurance industry from developing its own ways to cover terrorism losses.
